question: Can additive neural modules that each process a low-dimensional input projection avoid the exponential-in-input-dimension sample scaling assigned to a monolithic random-feature model, and can supervised kernel-norm minimization discover useful module projections before ordinary task training?

key_findings.claim: The first theoretical component derives closed-form expected train and test error for a ridgeless Gaussian random-feature regression model and reproduces an interpolation peak.
key_findings.evidence: Inputs are mapped to a d-by-P feature matrix with i.i.d. standard-Gaussian entries, the target is linear in an infinite coefficient vector with diagonal covariance, and the learner controls the first p coefficients through a minimum-norm interpolant. Theorem 1 expresses error through covariance traces, min(dn,p), and the expected squared Frobenius norm of a Gaussian pseudoinverse; this produces zero training error beyond the interpolation threshold and double-descent-like test error.

key_findings.claim: The exponential dependence on input dimension is inserted through a chosen target-spectrum parameterization rather than derived from the i.i.d. feature model.
key_findings.evidence: The input dimension m does not otherwise affect the Gaussian feature distribution. The paper sets lambda_i=c[i^(-Omega^(-m))-(i+1)^(-Omega^(-m))], making the target covariance's effective dimension approximately Omega^(2m), and then interprets this as manifold-volume scaling. On sine-wave networks, c, Omega, and an effective-parameter multiplier alpha are fit to observed training trends; the theory captures qualitative dependence and interpolation location but overpredicts the interpolation spike and underpredicts error at low data.

anchors.section: Appendix A.2, fitted effective parameter count

key_findings.claim: Theorem 2 intends to replace full input dimension m with module bottleneck dimension b, yielding an m-independent underparameterized error formula for additive modular tasks.
key_findings.evidence: The model sums K neural modules applied to m-by-b projections, and the target sums k corresponding low-dimensional functions. Linearization separates coefficients for projection matrices from coefficients internal to modules; the internal target spectrum is parameterized with b rather than m. The paper then claims that when dn>p, the m terms cancel and the samples needed for a target loss depend only on p, provided module parameter covariance is independent of m.

key_findings.claim: The dimension-independent conclusion does not follow from Theorem 1 under the modular model's own parameter count.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 10 says the controllable modular parameter vector has dimension mb+p: all mb projection coefficients plus p internal coefficients. Nevertheless, Theorem 2 uses F(dn,p), min(dn,p)/p, and the condition dn>p. A literal application of Theorem 1 must instead use q=mb+p in those rank and pseudoinverse terms. The appendix simultaneously includes mb in the controlled covariance trace but still leaves F and min indexed by p. With q, the underparameterized error contains F(dn,mb+p), and both the interpolation boundary and estimation factor depend on m; dimension independence therefore is not established as written.

anchors.section: Appendix C, controlled covariance includes mb projection coordinates
Appendix C, Theorem 2 substitution retains p in rank terms

key_findings.claim: The proposed practical intervention learns module initializations by minimizing the norm of an overparameterized kernel interpolant.
key_findings.evidence: For candidate projection U-hat, an expressive module feature map induces a conditional Gram matrix K. The minimum-norm coefficient size is y^T K^-1 y, so each module projection is initialized by gradient descent on that quantity from a different random start and all module parameters are subsequently trained on task loss. The rationale assumes pK>dn and that incorrect projections require larger interpolation norm; when the feature system is not overparameterized, the paper explicitly notes that lower coefficient norm need not imply lower prediction error. Kernel definitions are tailored separately to the linear sine, nonlinear distance-based sine, and flattened-image tasks.

key_findings.claim: On synthetic sine tasks, learned module initialization improves the tested sample-complexity curves and recovers target projection directions, but does not achieve the theory's exact dimension invariance.
key_findings.evidence: Across fully connected architectures and five seeds, the initialized modular networks require fewer samples than random modular and monolithic baselines as k=m grows; the authors explicitly report that empirical dependence on dimension remains because optimization becomes difficult. Learned projections attain higher maximum-cosine alignment with target directions and approach the performance of ground-truth projections, while freezing the learned initialization degrades results. On a nonlinear distance-projection variant at k=m=5, reported test loss is 0.393+/-0.099 versus 0.555+/-0.136 for random modular and 1.302+/-0.223 for monolithic networks.

key_findings.claim: Compositional CIFAR-10 supplies controlled combinatorial and noise-shift evidence, but the task exposes its block decomposition and gains disappear under large noise.
key_findings.evidence: Each example concatenates k flattened CIFAR-10 images into fixed 3072-coordinate blocks and predicts all k labels. With six components and disjoint train/test class combinations, the method reaches 49.90+/-0.15 percent accuracy versus 45.26+/-0.06 modular and 42.56+/-0.07 monolithic. With training-only Gaussian noise sigma=1, results are 46.95+/-0.11, 43.07+/-0.08, and 39.47+/-0.09 percent; from sigma=3 through 30, the proposed and random modular results are statistically close and sometimes reverse in point estimate. The architecture additionally shares all module weights, matching the fact that every component performs the same image-classification subtask.

method.core_idea: Model both monolithic and additive modular networks as ridgeless linear regression in infinite Gaussian features, assign target spectral complexity according to the dimension each network must process, and use minimum interpolation norm as a supervised signal for initializing module projections.
method.mechanism: For the theory, draw an i.i.d. Gaussian feature matrix, place a decaying prior covariance on target coefficients, and compute the minimum-norm interpolant's expected error with Gaussian pseudoinverse moments. In the modular construction, linearize both each m-by-b projection and each module's internal weights, sum module outputs, and assign internal spectra based on b. For learning, construct a task-specific module-conditional kernel for a candidate projection, repeatedly subsample labeled examples, differentiate y^T K^-1 y into the projection, initialize several modules from separate random starts, and then train the full modular network with Adam. Evaluate on additive sine functions and concatenated flattened CIFAR-10 images whose component labels form an additive target.
assumptions: Feature entries are i.i.d. unit Gaussians across coordinates and samples and the total feature count tends to infinity.
The target is linear in those features, has mean-zero coefficients, and has diagonal covariance with a hand-chosen spectral decay.
The learner finds the exact minimum-norm interpolating solution even though empirical networks are nonlinear and trained by finite-step Adam.
Input dimension affects target complexity through the selected covariance exponent, while other aspects of the random-feature distribution remain unchanged.
Tasks decompose as a sum of module outputs and each module receives a fixed-dimensional bottleneck b independent of global dimension m.
Linearization yields one shared Gaussian projection-feature map and one shared internal-feature map, so only sums of module parameters enter the theoretical model.
The module-conditional feature system is sufficiently expressive that pK exceeds dn and its Gram matrix is invertible or numerically stable.
Lower minimum interpolation norm reliably identifies a projection closer to a true task module.
The expected number and functional form of modules are known well enough to select K and design a problem-specific conditional kernel.
Extra labeled-data passes, kernel construction and inversion, and projection-search hyperparameters are available before ordinary task training.

techniques.role: Produces closed-form expected learning curves and an interpolation threshold.
Encodes an exponentially growing effective target dimension through covariance eigenvalue decay.
Represents module projections and internal weights as two blocks of linearized parameters.
Converts random-design interpolation error into F(n,p), with inverse-Wishart closed forms away from the threshold.
Uses y-transpose K-inverse y as a supervised objective for candidate module projections.
Measures whether projected examples can be fit with small coefficients under a task-tailored feature geometry.
Searches powers of two for the smallest training-set size reaching a chosen test error.
Scores whether each learned module direction aligns with some ground-truth sine direction.
Creates controlled high-dimensional additive classification by concatenating independently labeled image components.

evaluations.setting: Additive sine-wave regression with k modules, m-dimensional Gaussian inputs, k and m from 2 to 9, n from 100 to 100000, nine fully connected ReLU architectures, and five seeds
evaluations.metric: Training/test loss trends and sample size required to reach a selected error
evaluations.result: The fitted random-feature model captures qualitative k, m, p, and n trends and the interpolation location; learned modular initialization has the slowest empirical sample-complexity growth but remains dimension dependent
evaluations.baseline: Randomly initialized monolithic and modular fully connected networks, plus the fitted theoretical curve

evaluations.setting: Module recovery on sine regression with m=k=10 and separately learned candidate projections
evaluations.metric: Maximum absolute cosine similarity to ground-truth directions, t-SNE visualization, and downstream test loss
evaluations.result: Kernel-norm initialization clusters closer to true directions and approaches fixed ground-truth-module performance; freezing its projections is worse than fine-tuning them
evaluations.baseline: Random modular initialization before and after gradient training, fixed learned projections, and fixed true projections

evaluations.metric: Test mean-squared loss with standard error
evaluations.result: 0.393+/-0.099 for the proposed initialization versus 0.555+/-0.136 modular and 1.302+/-0.223 monolithic
evaluations.baseline: Randomly initialized modular and monolithic networks

evaluations.result: The proposed modules retain a visible accuracy advantage over both baselines at larger component counts and learn block-local projection weights

limitations: Author-stated: the closed-form analysis uses strong assumptions inherited from random-feature and ridgeless-regression theory and covers only a specific form of modularity.
Author-stated: theory assumes linear input projections and both theory and experiments assume additive module outputs; routing and flexible composition are left open.
Author-stated: empirical modular networks do not achieve the predicted dimension-independent sample complexity because high-dimensional optimization remains difficult.

Reviewer-identified: Theorem 2 counts a controllable vector of dimension mb+p but uses p in its pseudoinverse and rank factors, so its exact formula and headline dimension-independence conclusion do not follow from Theorem 1.

Reviewer-identified: exponential monolithic complexity and low-dimensional modular complexity are encoded by choosing different covariance spectra; they are not derived from the actual input geometry or neural architecture.

Reviewer-identified: the modular theory collapses all K projections and module weights into their sums under shared Gaussian feature maps, so it contains no module identity, routing, competition, collapse, specialization dynamics, or dependence on number of modules.

Reviewer-identified: the practical norm objective has only an intuition, not a consistency theorem showing that its minimizers recover true projections or improve population risk; the paper itself notes failure of the rationale outside interpolation.

Reviewer-identified: each task requires a bespoke kernel and a known or heavily overprovisioned module count; no selection rule is given for unknown, heterogeneous, overlapping, hierarchical, sequential, or interacting modules.

Reviewer-identified: the method adds repeated labeled-data passes, O(b cubed) Gram inversions, and projection optimization before task training, but comparisons do not report matched wall-clock, FLOPs, memory, or total optimization budget.

Reviewer-identified: hyperparameters are selected by lowest test error and no distinct validation split is described; dimension-specific early stopping and a censored maximum sample size further complicate sample-complexity comparisons.

Reviewer-identified: evidence is limited to two designed additive task families, dimensions at most nine or eight components, fully connected networks, and fixed block-aligned image concatenation; no natural compositional benchmark, Transformer, routed MoE, robotics, RL, or language task is evaluated.

Reviewer-identified: Compositional CIFAR-10 exposes module boundaries as fixed contiguous blocks and shares module weights because every subtask is identical, making the intended decomposition unusually easy and unlike unknown heterogeneous real-world modules.
Reviewer-identified: the main sample-complexity and accuracy evidence is curve based with five seeds and no statistical test; exact values are supplied only for the smaller supplemental studies.
Reviewer-identified: the noise-shift advantage vanishes at standard deviation three and above, so robustness is limited rather than uniform.
failure_modes: A task is not additively separable, so independently initialized module outputs cannot represent interactions without an additional composition or routing mechanism.
True module inputs grow with global dimension, invalidating the fixed-b bottleneck that creates the theoretical advantage.
Using the correct mb+p learnable-coordinate count moves the system toward the interpolation peak as m grows and restores dimension dependence.
The chosen target covariance is a poor model of real network spectral bias, so predicted scaling exponents do not transfer.
Several candidate projections converge to the same low-norm basin because the objective includes no explicit diversity or assignment constraint.
The conditional Gram matrix becomes singular or ill-conditioned, making y-transpose K-inverse y and its gradient unstable.
An incorrect projection supports a small-norm interpolant through spurious correlations, so norm minimization confidently initializes the wrong module.
The module count is misspecified: too few modules merge mechanisms, while too many increase search cost and enable redundant or collapsed modules.
A task-specific kernel omits the invariant that defines a real module, so initialization provides no benefit over random weights.
Kernel-search compute or label use exceeds the savings from reduced task-training samples.
Block position, rather than semantic module discovery, explains performance on concatenated images and fails when components overlap, translate, or interact.
Distribution shift corrupts the learned projection geometry, as suggested by convergence with the random modular baseline under high input noise.
reusable_insights: Separate the statistical benefit of a known low-dimensional decomposition from the optimization problem of discovering that decomposition.
Count projection, router, and expert parameters in the random-design matrix before claiming dimension-independent sample complexity.
Use minimum interpolation norm as a candidate representation-selection signal, but validate its population correlation and numerical conditioning.
Evaluate learned modules against ground-truth directions on controlled tasks as well as against downstream loss.
Compare learned initialization with fixed true modules to reveal the remaining optimization and representation gap.
Report unconditioned, combinatorial-holdout, and corruption-shift results separately because they probe different generalization claims.
Charge module discovery, routing, and kernel optimization to the total compute and labeled-sample budget.
Vary module count, module input dimension, interaction order, and boundary observability independently rather than tying k=m.
Test whether a purported modular gain survives when module boundaries are hidden and the monolithic baseline receives equivalent sharing or equivariance.
open_questions: What is the corrected generalization formula when all mb projection parameters are included, and what m-dependent sample rate follows?
Can one prove that minimizing y-transpose K-inverse y consistently identifies true module subspaces under finite data and noisy labels?
How should the objective be regularized or written with a pseudoinverse when K is ill-conditioned or the feature system is not interpolating?
Can diversity, sparsity, or assignment constraints prevent independently searched modules from collapsing to the same projection?
How can module number, bottleneck dimension, and conditional kernel be selected without ground-truth task structure or test-set tuning?
Do benefits persist under multiplicative interactions, hierarchies, temporal composition, overlapping supports, routing, and heterogeneous module types?
How does the method compare with meta-learned hypernetworks, patch-routed MoE, expert-choice routing, and end-to-end sparsity under matched compute?
Does learned modular initialization help convolutional, Transformer, RL, robotics, or language systems at dimensions and data scales where modern scaling laws are measured?
Can a dense network recover the same compositional behavior simply through scale and coverage, and when is explicit modularity more efficient?
Which observable signal distinguishes semantically correct module recovery from exploiting fixed input blocks or other shortcut structure?

competitive_landscape.title: Patch-level Routing in Mixture-of-Experts is Provably Sample-efficient for Convolutional Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: prior sample-complexity theory for modular routing
competitive_landscape.difference: Chowdhury et al. prove polynomial sample savings for patch-routed two-layer CNN experts when routers isolate class-discriminative patches, analyze separate and joint training, and test MNIST, CIFAR-10, CelebA, and Wide ResNets. The reviewed paper gives intended exact random-feature error formulas for additive low-dimensional modules and a projection initializer, but its dimension-count error undermines the stronger m-independent claim and it does not model routing.

competitive_landscape.title: Discovering modular solutions that generalize compositionally
competitive_landscape.difference: Schug et al. connect compositional generalization to identifying a modular teacher in hypernetworks, prove recovery up to linear transformation without observing exponentially many combinations, and meta-learn modular policies in several environments. That directly addresses hidden module discovery before this paper; the reviewed work instead optimizes a supervised kernel norm for additive input projections and tests regression plus concatenated images.

competitive_landscape.title: On The Specialization of Neural Modules
competitive_landscape.difference: Jarvis et al. analyze gradient dynamics of linear modules, formalize systematicity, identify when specialization succeeds or fails, and confirm trends in nonlinear networks and compositional datasets. The reviewed paper bypasses end-to-end specialization by learning projections before task training and focuses on sample scaling, but its theory collapses module identities and therefore does not describe the specialization process.

competitive_landscape.title: Is a Modular Architecture Enough?
competitive_landscape.difference: Mittal et al. systematically measure modular architectures on known modular distributions, expose optimization and module-collapse gaps, and introduce metrics for their unrealized potential. The reviewed work responds with a kernel-based initializer and an explicit learning-curve model, but only on additive tasks and without broad routing or collapse comparisons.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling can lead to compositional generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: Redhardt et al. show empirically that ordinary dense networks can acquire compositional generalization when data and model size scale with sufficient task-space coverage, and prove linear-width approximation for a class of compositional task families. This challenges a simple modular-versus-monolithic dichotomy: explicit modules may improve efficiency, but dense networks are not inherently barred from compositional structure.

competitive_landscape.title: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts for Compositional Generalization: Empirical Evidence and Theoretical Foundations of Optimal Sparsity
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhao et al. balance approximation and estimation error to predict an intermediate optimal number of active experts that grows with task complexity and varies with data and model complexity, validating it on symbolic reasoning and skill mixtures. Their result emphasizes adaptive sparsity rather than a fixed dimension-independent bottleneck and tests actual routed experts.

competitive_landscape.title: Generalization and Scaling Laws for Mixture-of-Experts Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: This work derives covering-number and ERM bounds that separate active expert capacity from routing combinatorics, including an explicit k log(eM/k) routing overhead and manifold-smoothness approximation term. In contrast, the reviewed theory has no router-combinatorics cost and assigns the modular advantage through a target covariance; the newer framework makes clear that inactive capacity and routing choices still affect estimation.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: this is the first work to give explicit non-asymptotic generalization-error expressions for modular neural networks, prove their sample complexity can be independent of task input dimension, and turn that insight into a module-alignment learning rule. Reviewer inference: the Gaussian-ridgeless synthesis, a projection-search objective based on minimum interpolation norm, and controlled tests linking alignment to downstream loss form a coherent contribution. Yet provable sample efficiency for routed experts, theoretical module specialization, and identification of hidden modular teachers all predate it, so the broad first-theory framing is too expansive. More critically, Theorem 2 applies a p-coordinate random-design formula to a model that explicitly controls mb+p coordinates. Correcting that count reintroduces m into F and the interpolation boundary, so the headline dimension-independent theorem is not currently supported. The practical initializer remains interesting, but evidence comes from bespoke additive kernels and highly structured synthetic tasks with extra unmatched search compute; it should be viewed as a promising supervised initialization heuristic rather than a demonstrated break of real neural scaling laws.
reviewer_notes: All 29 extracted pages were checked, including the full main text, both theorem proofs, Gaussian-pseudoinverse calculation, data and architecture definitions, kernel choices, hyperparameter sweeps, binary-search procedure, exact supplemental OOD tables, ablations, and projection visualizations. The mb+p versus p mismatch was additionally checked against rendered source-PDF pages 6-7 and the appendix, ruling out extraction ambiguity. Competitor identifiers and scopes were checked against current primary arXiv, OpenReview, NeurIPS, or official PMLR records through 2026-08-23.
